KM suggestions: One of two groups of nouns, often ‘it’ or ‘a thing.’

Informal explanation: the other thing, disambiguation of inanimate third persons
KM suggestions: Noun inflection marking third person inanimate thing as backgrounding to differentiate between two inanimate third person things. For example, “The keys on the table.” The table is backgrounded compared to the focus placed on the keys.
Two or more things belonging to the inanimate group of nouns, might be “many things.”
Pronouns referring to oneself. For example, “I teach high school. My students emailed me.”
Not inclusive (lister is removed from the group reference) for example, “We (not you) saw you at the park. You told us to visit the pond.”
Pronouns referring to the listener (singular). For example, “You are a student. Where do you go to school?”
The listener is included. For example, “Let’s tell someone what we just found.” The speaker is including the listener as part of the plural pronoun ‘we.’
Second person addressing a group (two or more) like forms in some varieties of English such as: youse/youse’s, y’all/y’all’s, you all/ you all’s, or you guys/you guy’s.
Pronouns referring to someone or something that isn’t the speaker or listener: he/him, she/her, it/its, and they/them (as a gender-neutral third person singular pronoun).

Informal explanation: the other one, disambiguation of third persons
KM suggestions: The third person that is not the focus is marked with inflection and becomes backgrounded to keep the attention on the (proximate) focused third person.

Informal explanation: the other _other_ one, disambiguation of third persons
KM suggestions: A way of distinguishing third persons. The noun (3rd person) with the obviative suffix is backgrounded. Further obviation makes another third person even further defocused. For example, “It was my dog that chased the squirrel past some kids!” The dog is most prominent, then the squirrel, and then the kids.
Pronouns referring to the third person for example, “The students were nervous. They had a test. I saw them cramming before class.”

There are time adverbs like ‘waabang,’ ‘tomorrow;’ location or place adverbs like ‘shaweyhiing,’ ‘alongside;’ manner adverbs like ‘gaawaanh,’ ‘barley;’ and circumstance adverbs like ‘njida,’ ‘on purpose,’ among other types of adverbs (Valentine 2001:138-147).

KM suggestions: The agent or “doer” of the verb stays the subject, but something like an object is removed (a semantic role is decreased), for example, “I ate (lunch).” An example is ‘gnaadmaage,’ ‘you (sg.) help’ (Valentine 2001:687).
Someone benefits from an action similar to “for” in English as in, “We carried boxes for her.” A X's for B.
Inflection indicating A makes B do X. For example, “I made my dog sit before getting a treat.”

Informal explanation: used in questions, relative clauses, if-then statements
KM suggestions: Verbal inflection for forming questions (who, what, etc., but not yes/no questions), if-then statements, and relative clauses (Valentine 2001:158). Verbs in conjunct order are subordinate to (supports) a main verb. Similar to, “I asked her to help me,” where ‘help’ supports the main verb ‘asked’ in English.

The contemptive gives nouns a degraded sense, expressing a speaker’s negative attitude towards them. Valentine gives examples like, “of no great value,” “just an ordinary,” and “I shouldn’t buy that crummy table” (Valentine 2001:185).
Elements like ‘and,’ ‘or,’ and ‘but,’ that link phrases or words.  ‘Miinwa’ and ‘gye’ are two common examples of coordinating words (coordinative adverbs) (Valentine 2001:996).
A delayed command such as “do it in a while!” Valentine gives the example of “Bi-zhaakan!” meaning “Come over later!” (Valentine 2001:222).

A noun ending that adds a quality of cuteness, smallness, and affection for X, like saying “doggie.” It can also mean a juvenile animal. Some nouns with a semantic meaning of smallness, like ‘baby,’ are always diminutive (Valentine 2001:494).

A noun ending indicating location that could mean ‘around,’ ‘among,’ or ‘in.’ The distributed locative is most often with “mass nouns,” things like ‘grass,’ ‘woods,’ ‘water,’ and ‘sand,’ that aren’t counted and are already plural in their meaning. For example, “His daughters are playing in the sand” (Valentine 2001:746).
Verbal inflection expressing the speaker is uncertain or doubts/questions something, like saying “supposedly” in English.

Informal explanation: the person prefix ni/gi/o- has been extended with da/di/doo
KM suggestions: Modern forms of the person prefixes that emerged from language change. Modern speakers lengthened (extended) forms to further define forms them as they were reduced by (syncope) the deletion of vowels.
The imperative order is verb inflection used for commands which includes immediate, delayed, and negative (prohibitive) commands.
Short one or two (adverbial particles) expressions conveying emotion, like ‘aa!,’ ‘come on!,’ ‘aambe!,’ ‘let’s (go)!,’ and ‘enh,’ ‘yes’ (Valentine 2001:149).

Particles are things that do not take inflection (things like plurality or animacy) as nouns and verbs do (Macaulay et al. 2026). Independent or “free” particles can appear on their own rather than needing to join a host (word).

Verbal inflection added to verbs in the conjunct order to express a repeated action. Could also be the relative preverb meaning ‘so many times,’ as in, ‘Endso-dgoshing,’ ‘every time he comes’ (Valentine 2001:801-802).
A noun ending indicating location (locative) that could mean ‘on,’ ‘in,’ or ‘at.’

One of the two groups (classes) of nouns. Generally, all living things are animate, but this does not always hold. Animacy has to be memorized by learners, as it is grammatical (agreement) and part of a speaker’s intuition of their first language.

KM suggestions: Some nouns must have a person possessing them (marked by a person prefix). These nouns are often body parts and family (kinship terms). It is not possible to just say ‘grandma,’ it has to be in relation to someone. For example, ‘nzid,’ ‘my foot’ (Valentine 2001:106).

One of the two groups (classes) of nouns, “it” or “a thing.” Inanimate nouns are generally non-living things, but this doesn’t always hold. Animacy has to be memorized by learners as it is grammatical (agreement) and part of a speaker’s intuition of their first language.

an obligatorily posessed

KM suggestions: Some nouns must have a person possessing them (marked by a person prefix). Dependent nouns are most often animate nouns like kinship terms. Some clothing items are among the examples of dependent inanimate nouns (Valentine 2001:113).

Negation (meaning not) is formed by two parts that work together, ‘gaawiin’ (sometimes gaa wii or just gaa) and ‘-sii’ (sometimes siiw), like in “Gaa wii dash gii-naagzisii,” ‘he was not visible’ (Valentine 2001:838). The pair becomes ‘gego’ (or gegwa) and ‘-ke(n)’ (or -siidaa) when giving a negative command like “don’t do X!”

Informal explanation: the syncope expected with person prefix o- did not occur, as if no prefix had been added
KM suggestions: A historical change that accounts for the difference between older person prefixes and the ones used by modern speakers that impacts vowel deletion. For example, ‘s/he works,’ ‘gidanokii,’ becoming ‘gnokii’ and the  o- is not deleted because the verb and prefix have changed.
Notes: A new style of prefix that would not be found on older versions of this word such as g- on 'gnokii' from the older form ‘gidanokii.’

KM suggestions: For example, ‘bezhig,’ ‘one,’ ‘niizh,’ ‘two,’ and nswi,’ ‘three,’ (Valentine 2001:874).

Informal explanation: a way of distinguishing third persons from each other where the third person with obviation morphology becomes defocused or backgrounded. The obviated third person is backgrounded/less central
KM suggestions: A way of distinguishing more than one third persons. One noun becomes backgrounded when it takes the “obviative” suffix. For example, “It was the child that watched some geese.” The child would be (proximate), making them the focus, while “some geese” would have the “obviate” suffix that backgrounds them.

Informal explanation: a way of distinguishing backgrounded third persons from each other
KM suggestions: A way of distinguishing third persons from each other where one noun gets marked obviative with a suffix, causing it to become defocused or backgrounded. Further obviation makes another third person even less focused/further backgrounded.
Notes: Small typo in the technical definition

KM suggestions: The first vowel of verb complex (will show up on tense if present) in the conjunct order (inflection forming dependent verbs) shows a predictable vowel change. For example, the past tense ‘gii’ becomes ‘gaa’ (Valentine 2001:511).
Removes focus from the “doer” of an action like in the examples, “The sink was cleaned” and ‘gii-miinaawag,’ ‘were given’ (Valentine 2001:688).
Similar to (gerund) “-ing forms” in English. Participles are (relative clauses) noun and verb like and made from any verb. For example, ‘nebaajig,’ ‘those who are sleeping’ (Valentine 2001:138).

A negative sense expressing strong dislike. Such as, “this darn cat” in the example, “Gegeti gsha maaba gaazhgenzhish! Mii miin waa naami-nbaagan gii-oo-miiziid!” meaning “Oh this darn cat! It’s gone and pooped under the bed again!” (Valentine 2001: 190).
Two or more. For example, ‘mtig,’ ‘tree’ and ‘mtigoog,’ ‘trees’ or ‘doopwin,’ ‘table’ (Valentine 2001:115).
“Have” or “own.” For example, ‘dayi,’ ‘have a dog’ and ‘niijaansi,’ ‘have a child’ (Valentine 2001:416).
Refers to someone or something, I/you/he/she/it/that/we/us/they/them. Also points to something with words like “this” or “these.”

Informal explanation: in verbs: X has been completed, in nouns: X is broken/deceased/no longer
KM suggestions: On verbs in the independent order, the suffix has a temporal effect (something was completed). Verbs in the conjunct get a counterfactual (if something hypothetically were to happen) reading (Rice 2023). On nouns it can mean past possession; most often is used to mark someone who has passed away like saying, “my late friend.”
Notes: APA Citation: Rice, M. (2023). The preterit mode and counterfactuality in Ojibwe. In M. Macaulay & M. Noodin (Eds.), Papers of the Fifty-Second Algonquian Conference (pp. 263–283). Michigan State University Press

KM suggestions: Words like ‘aanind,’ ‘some,’ ‘gkina (kina),’ ‘all,’ and ‘niibwa (niibna),’ ‘many’ (Valentine 2001:144).

Informal explanation: A and B do X to each other
KM suggestions: “They helped each other.” A and B do X to each other.

Informal explanation: indicates intensity, repetitiveness, plurality of subject, etc.
KM suggestions: Reduplication expresses things like intensity, repetitiveness, and plurality. For example, “It was cold cold!” (shows intensity) and “I saw mosquitos, mosquitos, mosquitos, everywhere” (shows plurality of the subject).

Informal explanation: A does X to A's self
KM suggestions: A reflexive is an action that is done to oneself. Reflexives are only formed by transitive animate verbs. A does X to A's self. For example, ‘Gziingwehdizo,’ ‘Wash/wipe one’s face’ (Valentine 2001: 408).

Informal explanation: -igoo/aa/ind', marks passive voice (prefix is patient) for VAIs derived from VTAs, often called an 'unspecified actor theme'
KM suggestions: When a transitive animate verb becomes an animate intransitive verb by passivation. Passive voice is marked by '-igoo/aa/ind' and the person prefix is the patient (experiences but does not do the action) often called an “unspecified actor theme” or “X” (Valentine 2001:272).

Technical definition: Intransitive Verb with an Animate subject
Informal explanation: description/action of a being or remarkable thing
KM suggestions: Verbs with animate subjects, for example, “s/he reads”. A few examples include, ‘zhiitaa,’ ‘ready,’ ‘dnizo,’ ‘cook there,’ and ‘oodetoo,’ ‘go to town’ (Valentine 2001:231).

Technical definition: Intransitive' Verb with an Animate subject and an Object
Informal explanation: action performed by a being or remarkable thing to something else
KM suggestions:
Verbs with animate subject and an optional object. For example, “s/he reads (a book).”
 
A few examples include, ‘miigwed,’ ‘give (object) away,’ ‘nokaazod,’ ‘use (something),’ and ‘gwid,’ ‘wear (something)’ (Valentine 2001:242).

Technical definition: Intransitive Verb with an Inanimate subject
KM suggestions:
Verbs with an inanimate subject. For example, weather verbs, often “it is/be”. 

A few examples include, ‘wiisgan,’ ‘be bitter,’ ‘mchaa,’ ‘be big,’ and ‘yaamgad,’ ‘be (there)’ (Valentine 2001:253).

Technical definition: Transitive Verb with an Animate object
Informal explanation: action performed on a being or remarkable thing
KM suggestions: Verbs with an animate object. For example, “Fred sees him” or ‘nwaabmaa,’ ‘I see her/him’ (Valentine 2001:279).

Technical definition: Transitive Verb with an Inanimate object
KM suggestions:
Verbs with an inanimate object. For example, “Fred sees it”.

A few examples include, ‘nda-bzindaan,’ ‘I listen to inanimate noun,’ ‘nda-mnwendaan,’ ‘I like IN,’ and ‘ndebwetaan,’ ‘I believe IN’ (Valentine 2001:309).

Set of terms for directly addressing/calling out to someone. A few examples include, ‘noose!,’ ‘my father,’ ‘ndoodoo!,’ ‘my mother,’ and ‘biidii!,’ ‘chicks (chicken and turkeys)’ (Valentine 2001:205-206).

Informal explanation: when prefixed: someone's X, when suffixed, I was X'ed (by someone), in Nishnaabemwin 'by someone' cannot be added
KM suggestions: X can be prefixed or suffixed and is like passive voice without changing the transitivity of the verb. In passive voice, the “actor” (agent) who does the action is removed, like in “The popcorn was eaten.” An unspecified actor is more like saying “Someone ate the popcorn.”
